summary.title: Choose Boring Technology
summary.one_liner: Pick a small set of well-understood, mature technologies over novel ones, because every new tool carries ongoing operational cost that usually outweighs its short-term benefit.
takeaways: Prefer mature, well-understood technology whose failure modes are known, and keep the number of tools in your stack small.
Innovation is a scarce resource (modeled as limited 'innovation tokens'), so spend it deliberately on what matters most.
Adding a new technology is easy but operating it well in production over time is hard; weigh ongoing maintenance cost against short-term gains.
Make technology choices a team conversation, starting with the question of how to solve the problem without adding anything new.
Master the tools you pick; the frustration of early use fades with expertise, and new tools are not automatically better.
summary.summary: This is a transcript of Dan McKinley's talk (adapted from his essay) on how engineering teams should choose technology. He draws on his experience at Etsy and later companies, using a cost-benefit model of technology choices, the distinction between known unknowns and unknown unknowns, and an activity-feed example where a shared, mature stack (Memcached and MySQL) scaled 20x without special attention. He argues for the smallest set of tools covering the problem domain, a team-level process for adding technology, and committing to replacing old tools rather than running redundant ones indefinitely.
